subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 14 periods = 560 minutes
Total: 14 periods · 9h 20min

periods.activity_title: Who Lives With Us? Opening the Picture Walk
periods.textbook_anchor: Living in Harmony — Students look at the picture of animals, birds, insects, and plants sharing human homes and discuss which of these live in their own homes (p. 73)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 72 picture spread of myna, hibiscus, dragonfly, cat, snail, goat, grasshopper, and potted plants

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 72 and invites the class to look silently at the picture spread — myna, hibiscus, dragonfly, cat, snail, goat, grasshopper, potted plants. Students name aloud what they notice.

Using Textbook p. 73, the teacher poses the question: 'Do any of these animals, birds, insects, and plants live with you in your house?' Students share in a whole-class discussion. Teacher records names of creatures mentioned on the board, grouping those that appeared in the picture separately from any the class adds spontaneously.

Discussion shifts to: 'Do you and your family take care of them?' Students share stories of feeding, watering, or sheltering a creature. Teacher gently draws out whether the animal or plant was invited or arrived on its own, building the invited-versus-uninvited distinction on the board.

Teacher closes the discussion by asking: 'Which of these creatures at home did your grandparents or elders also keep when they were young?' Students share briefly. Teacher notes that different families across India keep different creatures, celebrating this diversity before the unit ends.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe relationships between their families and living beings in their immediate environment, drawing on personal and intergenerational experience.
periods.section_context: Myna, hibiscus, dragonfly, cat, snail, goat, grasshopper, potted plants; invited versus uninvited living beings in the home; family care practices for animals and plants.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask an open question such as: 'Did your grandmother or grandfather keep an animal that you have never kept yourself?' This draws out intergenerational knowledge naturally. Keep the pace conversational and unhurried so quieter students find space to speak.

periods.textbook_anchor: Living in Harmony — Students discuss which uninvited animals, birds, and insects visit their homes and how they feel about their presence (p. 74)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 74 and frames the focus: 'Some creatures come to our homes without being invited.' Students are asked to name the uninvited visitors they have seen — mosquitoes, lizards, spiders, ants, pigeons, mice, crows, etc. — and the teacher lists these on the board.

Discussion: 'Why do you think they come to your homes?' Students hypothesise — food, warmth, shelter, water. Teacher encourages reasoning ('What does an ant need that your kitchen has?') rather than single-word answers, and writes key reasons beside the creature's name on the board.

Discussion continues through the questions on Textbook p. 74: 'How do you feel about their presence?' and 'Which of them do you like?' Students explore mixed feelings — fear of spiders, delight in butterflies, irritation at mosquitoes. Teacher validates that it is natural to have different feelings toward different creatures.

Final discussion thread: 'What do you do when you do not like them?' Teacher steers the conversation toward responses that do not involve harming the creature — shooing away, closing windows, using nets — building a gentle behavioural norm of non-harm without labelling it.

periods.implied_lo: Students can articulate reasons why living beings share human spaces and reflect on a range of human feelings and responses toward them.
periods.section_context: Uninvited animals, birds, and insects in the home; reasons for their arrival; feelings of like, dislike, fear, and delight; responses and behavioural choices toward uninvited creatures.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Is there any creature you were once scared of but now find interesting?' This opens up the idea that our feelings can change when we understand a creature better. Allow disagreement among students — some may want to harm uninvited animals; use that as a teaching moment about co-existence.

periods.activity_title: Spot and Record: Animals Around Me
periods.textbook_anchor: Living in Harmony — Students find animals, birds, and insects they have spotted that are not in the picture on page 72, and record their names and where they were seen in the table (p. 73)
materials: Notebook or table in the textbook
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 72 picture spread used as a reference checklist

time_bands.activity: Teacher reopens Textbook p. 72 and asks the class to scan the picture carefully and mentally list everything shown. She then poses the Find out task from Textbook p. 73: 'Are there animals, birds, or insects you have spotted that are NOT in this picture? Let's find out and record them.'

Students work individually, recalling creatures they have seen at home, on the way to school, in a garden, or in the fields. They fill in the table on Textbook p. 73 — creature name and where they saw it. Teacher circulates, helping with spellings and encouraging students to think beyond common examples.

Teacher invites volunteers to share one creature from their table. As each is named, classmates who also saw the same creature raise their hands. Teacher compiles a combined class list on the board, noting the variety of locations — rooftop, pond, tree, kitchen, courtyard, road.

Brief reflection: Teacher asks, 'Did anyone spot something that surprised the class — something unusual or rare?' Students share. Teacher closes by noting that the class together has spotted many more creatures than the textbook picture could show, linking observation to the richness of the living world around them.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record living beings in their immediate environment, noting the name and location of each.
periods.section_context: Animals, birds, and insects spotted by students beyond those shown on p. 72; locations of sightings — home, garden, road, pond, field; the class-compiled record of local living beings.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Where do you think that creature goes at night — does it stay near your home or travel far?' This extends observation into curiosity about habitat and behaviour without requiring a formal answer. Pair a student who has little to write with a more talkative partner for the recall phase.

periods.activity_title: The Mango Tree: A Home for Many
periods.textbook_anchor: The Mango Tree — Students discuss how plants help animals and how animals help plants, using the story of Shambhu and his father under the mango tree (p. 77)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 75–76 story illustrations and the radial diagram of uses of plants on p. 77

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the story of Shambhu and his father sitting under the mango tree from Textbook pp. 75–76, with expression. Students listen with books open. After reading, teacher asks: 'What did Shambhu's father say about the monkey and the mango seed?' Students retell in their own words.

Teacher directs students to the radial diagram on Textbook p. 77 showing the uses of the mango tree — shade, wood, medicine, fibre, fruit, fresh air, shelter for animals. Discussion: 'How are we dependent on plants and animals?' Students connect the diagram's spokes to things in their own lives (medicine from plants, wood for their home, fruit they eat).

Discussion continues from Textbook p. 77: 'How do plants help animals? How do animals help plants?' Teacher builds a two-column board chart. Students contribute: plants give food, shelter, nesting sites (plants help animals); animals disperse seeds, fertilise soil with waste (animals help plants). The monkey-seed example from the story anchors the second column.

Final question from Textbook p. 77: 'How do you look after plants and animals in your surroundings?' Students share personal practices — watering a tree, feeding birds, not breaking branches. Teacher closes by asking whether anyone's family has a particular tree they care for, drawing in local cultural connections to trees.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain the mutual relationships between plants and animals using examples drawn from a story and a diagram.
periods.section_context: Mango tree as multi-species habitat; birds, squirrels, monkeys as tree residents; monkey eating mango and dispersing seed; radial diagram of plant uses — shade, wood, medicine, fibre, fruit, fresh air, shelter for animals; human dependence on plants and animals.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Can you think of another tree near your home or school that gives home to many creatures — not just a mango tree?' This extends the mango tree example to the students' own local environment. If a student mentions a neem, peepal, or banyan tree, invite the class to name who lives in it.

periods.textbook_anchor: The Mango Tree — Students discuss how animals and plants depend on us and how we look after them, connecting to the uses-of-plants diagram (p. 77)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 77 radial diagram of uses of plants

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly revisits the radial diagram on Textbook p. 77 and the discussion from the previous unit's content about how humans, plants, and animals are connected. She then poses the creative task: 'Draw your own web — put yourself in the centre, and draw lines to all the plants and animals you depend on, and all the ones that depend on you.'

Students draw their personal interdependence web on a notebook page or drawing paper. Each line is labelled with the relationship — 'gives milk', 'gives shade', 'I water it', 'spreads seeds'. Teacher circulates, prompting students who are stuck: 'What did you eat this morning? Which plant or animal gave you that?' and 'Which creature at home depends on you to feed it?'

Four or five students share their webs with the class, placing them on the board or holding them up. Class notices similarities and differences — some students have cows, some have goats; some have mango trees, some have coconut palms. Teacher highlights that the web is different in different regions but the idea of mutual dependence is the same everywhere.

Quick closing discussion from Textbook p. 77: 'How do animals and plants depend on us?' Students give one example each. Teacher notes the two directions — what we receive, what we give — and affirms that this two-way care is what the chapter calls harmony.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent their personal relationships of mutual dependence with plants and animals through a labelled diagram.
periods.section_context: Five-way interdependence between humans, plants, and animals; students' personal webs of dependence; milk from cows, buffaloes, goats; shade, fruit, wood, medicine from plants; watering and feeding as human care; regional variation in plants and animals named.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'Did you put something on your web that no one else in the class put?' Celebrate unusual or regional examples such as silk from silkworms, honey from bees, or reeds for basket-weaving. These varied responses reveal the cultural strand of the chapter.

periods.activity_title: We Need Each Other: Mutual Dependence in Detail
periods.textbook_anchor: We Need Each Other — Students discuss mutual dependence: humans providing care, protection, food and shelter to animals and plants, and receiving food, fibre, companionship in return (p. 78)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 78 and introduces the section title 'We Need Each Other'. She reads the introductory text aloud. Class discussion: 'What do we give to animals — and what do animals give to us?' Teacher draws a simple two-column table on the board: 'We give to animals / Animals give to us'.

Students contribute to both columns through discussion. 'We give' column fills with: food, water, shelter, protection, care. 'Animals give us' column fills with: milk, wool, help in farming, companionship. Teacher adds the 'Do you know?' panel insight from Textbook p. 78 about squirrels burying and forgetting nuts — resulting in new trees — as an example of animals helping plants and humans without intending to.

Discussion continues: 'How do animals help plants?' Students recall from the mango tree story — seed dispersal by monkeys, soil fertility from animal waste. Teacher adds the squirrel example. The board chart grows to include 'Animals help plants / Plants help animals'. Students see the web expanding into a full circle of mutual need.

Teacher closes with a synthesis question: 'If we remove one part of this circle — for example, if there were no animals — what would happen to plants? What would happen to us?' Students reason through the consequences briefly. Teacher affirms that this is the meaning of 'we need each other' and that the chapter is about noticing and honouring these connections.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe specific ways in which humans, animals, and plants provide for each other's needs, forming a circle of mutual dependence.
periods.section_context: Humans giving food, water, shelter, protection to animals and plants; animals giving milk (cows, buffaloes, goats), fibre, companionship; squirrels burying and forgetting nuts leading to new trees; seed dispersal; soil fertility through animal waste; consequences of removing one part of the web.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does anyone's family keep a cow or goat? What does your family give it every day — and what does it give your family?' This personal grounding makes the two-way flow of need concrete. The squirrel example is a good moment to ask whether anyone has noticed a tree growing in an unexpected place — a crack in a wall, the edge of a roof.

periods.activity_title: Get to Know an Animal: Sustained Observation in Pairs
periods.textbook_anchor: We Need Each Other — Students choose an animal they see often and observe it closely, noting its behaviour, movement, and sounds (p. 78)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Activity 1 from Textbook p. 78 aloud: 'Get to Know an Animal.' She explains that students will choose one animal or bird they see regularly — a goat, crow, sparrow, cat, dog, pigeon, parrot, or duck — and become its careful observer. Students are given a moment to decide silently which creature they will choose and why.

Students open their notebooks and draw a simple observation frame with the questions from Textbook p. 78 as headers: Name of animal; Where and when I first saw it; Was it alone or with others; How it moves; Sounds it makes; What I saw it doing; Something that surprised or amused me. Students begin writing from memory about their chosen creature, drawing on what they already know.

Students share in pairs — each reads their observation notes aloud to a partner. Partners ask one question each: 'Did you see it eating?' or 'What sound did it make?' This oral exchange fills gaps in each student's notes. Teacher circulates and notes interesting observations to highlight with the class.

Three or four students share one surprising or amusing thing their animal did. Teacher acknowledges each story warmly and notes: 'These are real observations — you are already thinking like naturalists.' She closes by encouraging students to keep watching their chosen creature in the days ahead and adding to their notes.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe a familiar animal closely and record its behaviour, movement, and sounds using a structured set of questions.
periods.section_context: Chosen animal: goat, cow, dog, cat, crow, pigeon, sparrow, parrot, or duck; observation categories — location, companions, movement, sounds, feeding, social behaviour, surprising actions; written observation notes.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Did your animal do something that you did not expect — something that made you think it was clever or funny?' Unexpected behaviour is the richest observation and builds genuine curiosity. If students choose the same animal, group them so they can compare whether they noticed different things about the same species.

periods.activity_title: Writing My Animal Story: From Observation to Expression
periods.textbook_anchor: We Need Each Other — Students write a short description of the animal or bird they have chosen, covering its appearance, movement, sounds, behaviour, and something surprising (p. 78)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the Write task from Textbook p. 78 aloud, going through each prompt: name and describe the animal; when and where first seen; alone or with friends; movement; sounds; eating, sleeping, interacting; something surprising or funny; share the story. Teacher models one or two sentences on the board to show what a vivid animal description sounds like.

Students write their short animal story in their notebooks, working from the observation notes they built in the previous activity on this section. Teacher circulates and nudges students who are writing single-word answers to add one more detail: 'How did it move — did it hop, strut, or dart?' She ensures every student reaches at least four of the seven prompts.

Students share their stories with the class as described in Textbook p. 78. Three or four volunteers read aloud; the class listens for one detail they found surprising or beautiful. After each reading, one classmate shares what stood out for them — building an appreciative listening culture.

Teacher closes by noting that every story is different because every student watched a different creature — and this variety of creatures around us is itself something to celebrate. She asks one quick question: 'Does this animal need something from us? What could you do for it?' planting the seed of care.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present their observations of a living being through a written descriptive account that includes behaviour, movement, sound, and personal response.
periods.section_context: Written animal portrait: appearance, location of first sighting, companions, movement, sounds, feeding and sleeping behaviour, social interactions, surprising or amusing actions; oral sharing of the written story with classmates.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Is there one sentence in your story that you are especially proud of — one that paints a picture?' Having students identify their own best writing builds confidence and awareness of craft. Allow students who prefer to draw their animal first and then write around the drawing.

periods.activity_title: Busy, Busy, Clever Ants: Predict and Observe
periods.textbook_anchor: We Need Each Other — Students place three types of food in a line, make guesses about ant behaviour, and then observe the outcome (p. 79)
materials: Small portions of sweet food (sugar or jaggery)
Small portions of fried food (papad or murukku)
Small portions of cooked food (bread, chapati, idli, rice, or ragi)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces Activity 2 from Textbook p. 79: 'Busy, Busy, Busy and Clever Ants!' She reads the setup: three types of food placed in a straight line with one foot between them — sweet, fried, and cooked. She reads the eight guess questions aloud and students write their predictions in their notebooks before any food is placed.

Students (in small groups or as a class, depending on classroom floor space) set up the three food items on the classroom floor or a clean outdoor area near the classroom. Teacher ensures the line is near a likely ant trail. Students note the starting time and make their last predictions.

Students observe the food line in an unhurried observation period, watching for ants and noting: which food ants go to first; whether all ants look the same; how many come; what they do with the food (carry, taste, swarm). Students record observations in their notebooks as they watch. Teacher circulates quietly, encouraging students to notice details beyond the obvious.

Class reconvenes and compares predictions with observations from Textbook p. 79. Teacher asks: 'Were your guesses correct? What surprised you? What did the ants do that you did not expect?' Students discuss. Teacher closes by asking: 'What does the ants' choice of food tell us about what they need?' — connecting the inquiry back to the theme of animal needs.

periods.implied_lo: Students can perform a simple prediction-and-observation inquiry, recording what they expected and what they actually saw, and discussing the difference.
periods.section_context: Ant behaviour experiment: three food types — sweet (sugar or jaggery), fried (papad or murukku), cooked (bread, chapati, idli, rice, ragi); eight prediction questions; observation of which food ants prefer, ant appearance, number, and food-carrying behaviour; comparison of prediction with outcome.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask before the food is placed: 'Why do you think ants might prefer one food over another — what do you think ants need from food?' This ensures predictions are reasoned, not random. If ants do not arrive quickly, use the waiting time to revisit the predictions and ask students to refine them — 'Would you change your guess now? Why?'

periods.activity_title: Visiting Your Plant Friend: Empathy and Mime
periods.textbook_anchor: Visiting your Plant Friend — Students play the 'Guess Who I Am?' pair mime game, acting as an animal, bird, insect, or tree for the class to identify (p. 80)
materials: Open floor space for mime activity

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the opening of Textbook p. 80 aloud: visiting a plant friend when feeling sad, happy, or upset; talking to it; understanding that plants and animals also need our care. A brief discussion: 'Have you ever sat near a tree or plant when you needed to feel calm? What was it like?' Two or three students share personal moments.

Teacher introduces Activity 3 from Textbook p. 80: 'Guess Who I Am?' She explains the rules — sit in pairs, one partner whispers an animal, bird, insect, or tree name in the other's ear, the second partner mimes the creature's movement for the class to guess, then roles switch.

The mime game runs. Teacher cycles through pairs, giving each performing student a turn in front of the class or ensuring small-group rounds if the class is large. Students who watch call out their guesses. Teacher celebrates especially creative mimes — a snail's slow glide, a dragonfly's darting, a tree swaying in wind — naming what made them vivid.

Teacher reads the closing statement from Textbook p. 80 aloud: 'Plants also need our care and support. So do animals. We can all help each other.' Brief sharing: 'Which creature was the hardest to mime — and why?' Students reflect on what they had to know about a creature's body or movement in order to mime it well, connecting physical expression to observation.

periods.implied_lo: Students can express their knowledge of living beings through bodily mime, demonstrating awareness of distinctive movements and characteristics.
periods.section_context: Visiting a plant friend when feeling emotions; talking to plants; 'Guess Who I Am?' mime game; animals, birds, insects, and trees mimed; empathy toward plants and animals as co-dependents needing care.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask after a mime: 'What did you have to think about to perform that creature — how it moves its legs, wings, or leaves?' This metacognitive question makes the connection between close observation and creative expression explicit. Include the 'tree swaying in wind' option so students who are less confident with animal movement have an accessible choice.

periods.activity_title: The Valparai Wagtail: Community Harmony with Nature
periods.textbook_anchor: Visiting your Plant Friend — Students read about the Grey Wagtail welcome tradition in Valparai and discuss what it shows about community relationships with nature (p. 80)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 80 'Do you know?' panel about the Grey Wagtail of Valparai

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the 'Do you know?' panel from Textbook p. 80 aloud: school children and teachers in Valparai, Tamil Nadu, track the arrival of migratory Grey Wagtails (Vaalatti kuruvi) every winter, put up welcome posters, and distribute sweets to celebrate. Students listen and then share their first reactions: 'What do you find most surprising or beautiful about this?'

Discussion: 'Why do you think those children and teachers do this every year?' Students reason — they care for the bird; they are happy it returns; they want it to feel welcome. Teacher draws out the idea that this is a community tradition — something done together, year after year, linking people and nature in a seasonal rhythm.

Teacher asks: 'Does your community or family have any practice or tradition that celebrates or welcomes a particular animal, bird, or season?' Students share examples — feeding crows during ancestral rituals, releasing fish in rivers during festivals, planting trees on certain occasions, the arrival of the first monsoon rains. Teacher records examples on the board, celebrating regional diversity.

Teacher closes with a question: 'What would happen in Valparai if the Grey Wagtail stopped coming — how would the people feel? Why?' Students reflect on the emotional bond between communities and the natural world. Teacher affirms that harmony is not just between individuals but between whole communities and the living world they share.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe a community cultural practice connected to the natural world and explain the relationship between human care and seasonal natural events.
periods.section_context: Grey Wagtail (Vaalatti kuruvi); Valparai, Tamil Nadu; winter migration; school children and teachers making welcome posters and distributing sweets; community traditions celebrating the arrival of birds or seasons; students' own regional examples of nature-linked practices.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Why do you think they give the bird a Tamil name — Vaalatti kuruvi — rather than just calling it a wagtail?' This surfaces the idea that naming a creature in one's own language is a sign of closeness and belonging. Accept all regional examples students offer without ranking them — a fishing community welcoming the monsoon has as much cultural depth as the Valparai tradition.

periods.activity_title: Let Us Reflect: Dependence, Care, and Personal Connection
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students discuss how we depend on plants and animals and how we should care for them, then complete personal sentence frames expressing connection to living beings (p. 81)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 81. She reads the three discussion questions aloud: 'How are we dependent on plants and animals? How should we care for them? How do plants and animals depend on us?' Students discuss briefly in pairs, then share with the whole class. Teacher uses the board to capture the key ideas that emerge — a quick consolidation of the chapter's central ecological and ethical message.

Students work individually on the Write task from Textbook p. 81: completing the four sentence frames — 'I like looking at ___ because ___'; '___ make me laugh because ___'; 'My friend ___ likes ___ because ___'; 'I would like to take care of ___ because ___'. Teacher reminds students to use names of real plants, birds, animals, or insects they have personally encountered, not imagined ones.

Students share two or three of their completed sentences aloud. Teacher listens for the care-reasoning in the final sentence — 'I would like to take care of ___ because ___' — and highlights responses that show genuine empathy or responsibility, such as 'I would like to take care of the sparrow because it has lost its forest' or 'I would like to take care of my plant because it gives me flowers every morning.'

Teacher closes with a quiet moment: 'Think of one living being — plant, animal, bird, or insect — that you will actually do something for this week. You do not need to say it aloud. Just hold it in your mind.' This plants a personal behavioural intention without prescribing it.

periods.implied_lo: Students can articulate personal reasons for caring about specific living beings and express a sense of responsibility toward them.
periods.section_context: Three reflection discussion questions on dependence and care; four sentence-completion frames — looking at, making laugh, friend's connection, wanting to care for; real plants, animals, birds, insects named by students; personal care intentions.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Did anyone write something in the last sentence frame that surprised even yourself — something you had not thought about caring for before today?' This reflective question surfaces genuine moral growth. Ensure the sentence-completion task is personal rather than generic — redirect answers like 'I would like to take care of trees' toward something specific: 'Which tree? Where is it? What will you do for it?'

periods.activity_title: Ranking and Classifying: Smallest to Largest and by Leg Count
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students write the names of all animals, birds, and insects from smallest to largest, and draw and name creatures categorised by number of legs (p. 81–82)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the Write task from Textbook p. 81 aloud: 'Write down the names of all the animals, birds, insects that you have seen or learned about — from the smallest to the largest.' Students begin individually, writing a personal ranked list. Teacher encourages them to think across all the creatures they have discussed throughout the chapter, including from their own observation records.

Students share their ranked lists with a partner and compare: 'Do you have creatures in your list that I do not have? Did we rank them in the same order?' Partners discuss any disagreements — is an ant smaller than a snail? Is a crow larger than a pigeon? Teacher circulates and encourages students to reason about size from their observations rather than just guessing.

Students move to the Draw task from Textbook p. 82: Name and draw animals, birds, and insects with two legs, four legs, six legs, and eight legs. Students set up four sections in their notebooks and draw at least one creature per category. Teacher circulates, asking: 'How many legs does a spider have? Does a worm have legs at all?' — prompting careful thinking about classification.

Quick class check: teacher calls out each leg category and students name creatures from their drawings. The class builds a combined list on the board for each category. Teacher notes any interesting cases — a caterpillar has many legs; a snake has none — and invites students to keep noticing leg-counts on creatures they encounter.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify living beings by an observable physical feature — number of legs — and order familiar creatures by relative size.
periods.section_context: Students' personal ranked list of animals, birds, and insects from smallest to largest; classification by leg count — two legs (birds), four legs (goat, cat, dog, cow), six legs (ants, grasshoppers), eight legs (spiders); drawings in four categories.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'How did you decide which creature was smallest — did you compare their bodies, or their length from nose to tail? Does it change the ranking?' This surfaces the idea that size is a measurable but complex property. Accept multiple valid rankings as long as students can give a reason for their ordering.

periods.activity_title: Favourite Living Being: My Creature, My Reasons
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students identify their favourite animal, bird, insect, or plant and write about why they like it (p. 81)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the two questions from Textbook p. 81 aloud: 'Which is your favourite animal, bird, insect, or plant among those you have named? Why do you like it?' She gives students a quiet moment to think — no writing yet, just genuine reflection. She then invites three students to share their choice aloud before any writing begins, to warm up the room.

Students draw their favourite living being on a page or in their notebook — a full drawing with colour — and write three to five sentences explaining why they chose it. The writing should go beyond 'it is beautiful' to reasons tied to what the creature does, how it behaves, what it gives, or how it makes the student feel. Teacher circulates and nudges toward richer reasons: 'What does it do that you find amazing? Does it do something for you or for other creatures?'

Students share in a gallery-walk format or by holding up their drawings while reading their sentences aloud. After each sharing, the class offers one appreciative observation. Teacher uses the sharing to draw out the variety of connections — some students chose a creature for its beauty, others for its usefulness, others for emotional companionship — showing the many forms that living in harmony can take.

Teacher reads the final line from Textbook p. 80 aloud once more: 'We can all help each other.' She closes the chapter with the question: 'Looking at all our drawings together — how many different living beings are represented in this classroom today? Does that tell you something about the world we live in?' No formal answer is required — the question is an invitation to wonder.

periods.implied_lo: Students can express a personal connection to a specific living being through drawing and writing, giving reasons rooted in observation and relationship.
periods.section_context: Students' chosen favourite animal, bird, insect, or plant; drawn portrait; written reasons — beauty, behaviour, usefulness, emotional connection; gallery sharing; variety of choices across the class as evidence of biodiversity in students' environments.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Can you write one reason that has to do with something the creature does — not just how it looks?' This pushes past aesthetic preference toward ecological or relational reasoning. Honour unusual choices — a student who chose an ant or a snail over a puppy is showing genuine independent thinking.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe relationships between their families and living beings in their immediate environment, drawing on personal and intergenerational experience.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Myna, hibiscus, dragonfly, cat, snail, goat, grasshopper, potted plants; invited versus uninvited living beings in the home; family care practices for animals and plants.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Living in Harmony — Students look at the picture of animals, birds, insects, and plants sharing human homes and discuss which of these live in their own homes (p. 73)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students examine the p. 72 picture spread, discuss which creatures live in their homes and whether families care for them, and share intergenerational stories about animals and plants kept by elders.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can articulate reasons why living beings share human spaces and reflect on a range of human feelings and responses toward them.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Uninvited animals, birds, and insects in the home; reasons for their arrival; feelings of like, dislike, fear, and delight; responses and behavioural choices toward uninvited creatures.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Living in Harmony — Students discuss which uninvited animals, birds, and insects visit their homes and how they feel about their presence (p. 74)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students name and list uninvited home visitors, hypothesise why they come, explore their mixed feelings about these creatures, and discuss responses that avoid harm.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can observe and record living beings in their immediate environment, noting the name and location of each.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Animals, birds, and insects spotted by students beyond those shown on p. 72; locations of sightings — home, garden, road, pond, field; the class-compiled record of local living beings.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Living in Harmony — Students find animals, birds, and insects they have spotted that are not in the picture on page 72, and record their names and where they were seen in the table (p. 73)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students individually fill in the p. 73 table with creatures they have spotted beyond the textbook picture, then pool their lists to build a class record of local living beings with locations.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain the mutual relationships between plants and animals using examples drawn from a story and a diagram.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Mango tree as multi-species habitat; birds, squirrels, monkeys as tree residents; monkey eating mango and dispersing seed; radial diagram of plant uses — shade, wood, medicine, fibre, fruit, fresh air, shelter for animals; human dependence on plants and animals.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: The Mango Tree — Students discuss how plants help animals and how animals help plants, using the story of Shambhu and his father under the mango tree (p. 77)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Teacher reads the Shambhu story aloud; students examine the p. 77 radial diagram and discuss five-way dependence between humans, plants, and animals, including seed dispersal by monkeys.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can represent their personal relationships of mutual dependence with plants and animals through a labelled diagram.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Five-way interdependence between humans, plants, and animals; students' personal webs of dependence; milk from cows, buffaloes, goats; shade, fruit, wood, medicine from plants; watering and feeding as human care; regional variation in plants and animals named.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: The Mango Tree — Students discuss how animals and plants depend on us and how we look after them, connecting to the uses-of-plants diagram (p. 77)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students draw a personal interdependence web with themselves at the centre, labelling each line with the relationship, then share their webs and note regional variation across the class.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe specific ways in which humans, animals, and plants provide for each other's needs, forming a circle of mutual dependence.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Humans giving food, water, shelter, protection to animals and plants; animals giving milk (cows, buffaloes, goats), fibre, companionship; squirrels burying and forgetting nuts leading to new trees; seed dispersal; soil fertility through animal waste; consequences of removing one part of the web.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: We Need Each Other — Students discuss mutual dependence: humans providing care, protection, food and shelter to animals and plants, and receiving food, fibre, companionship in return (p. 78)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students build a two-column class chart of what humans give animals and what animals give humans, then extend it to include animal-plant relationships, including the squirrel-nut-tree example.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can observe a familiar animal closely and record its behaviour, movement, and sounds using a structured set of questions.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Chosen animal: goat, cow, dog, cat, crow, pigeon, sparrow, parrot, or duck; observation categories — location, companions, movement, sounds, feeding, social behaviour, surprising actions; written observation notes.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: We Need Each Other — Students choose an animal they see often and observe it closely, noting its behaviour, movement, and sounds (p. 78)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students choose a familiar animal, complete a structured observation frame in their notebooks from memory and experience, share notes in pairs, and present one surprising observation to the class.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can present their observations of a living being through a written descriptive account that includes behaviour, movement, sound, and personal response.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Written animal portrait: appearance, location of first sighting, companions, movement, sounds, feeding and sleeping behaviour, social interactions, surprising or amusing actions; oral sharing of the written story with classmates.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: We Need Each Other — Students write a short description of the animal or bird they have chosen, covering its appearance, movement, sounds, behaviour, and something surprising (p. 78)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students write a short descriptive story about their chosen animal following the p. 78 prompts, then share their stories aloud and listen for one detail that stands out.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can perform a simple prediction-and-observation inquiry, recording what they expected and what they actually saw, and discussing the difference.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Ant behaviour experiment: three food types — sweet (sugar or jaggery), fried (papad or murukku), cooked (bread, chapati, idli, rice, ragi); eight prediction questions; observation of which food ants prefer, ant appearance, number, and food-carrying behaviour; comparison of prediction with outcome.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: We Need Each Other — Students place three types of food in a line, make guesses about ant behaviour, and then observe the outcome (p. 79)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students set up the Busy Ants experiment with three food types, write predictions for eight questions, observe ant responses over an unhurried period, then compare predictions with outcomes.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can express their knowledge of living beings through bodily mime, demonstrating awareness of distinctive movements and characteristics.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Visiting a plant friend when feeling emotions; talking to plants; 'Guess Who I Am?' mime game; animals, birds, insects, and trees mimed; empathy toward plants and animals as co-dependents needing care.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Visiting your Plant Friend — Students play the 'Guess Who I Am?' pair mime game, acting as an animal, bird, insect, or tree for the class to identify (p. 80)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students read the plant-friend concept, then play the 'Guess Who I Am?' mime game in pairs, with classmates guessing the creature, reflecting on what they needed to know to mime it well.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe a community cultural practice connected to the natural world and explain the relationship between human care and seasonal natural events.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Grey Wagtail (Vaalatti kuruvi); Valparai, Tamil Nadu; winter migration; school children and teachers making welcome posters and distributing sweets; community traditions celebrating the arrival of birds or seasons; students' own regional examples of nature-linked practices.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Visiting your Plant Friend — Students read about the Grey Wagtail welcome tradition in Valparai and discuss what it shows about community relationships with nature (p. 80)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Teacher reads the Valparai Grey Wagtail 'Do you know?' panel; students discuss why the tradition exists and share their own community practices celebrating or welcoming animals, birds, or seasons.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can articulate personal reasons for caring about specific living beings and express a sense of responsibility toward them.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Three reflection discussion questions on dependence and care; four sentence-completion frames — looking at, making laugh, friend's connection, wanting to care for; real plants, animals, birds, insects named by students; personal care intentions.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students discuss how we depend on plants and animals and how we should care for them, then complete personal sentence frames expressing connection to living beings (p. 81)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students discuss three reflection questions, complete four personal sentence frames about living beings they love and want to care for, then share and hold a private care intention.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify living beings by an observable physical feature — number of legs — and order familiar creatures by relative size.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Students' personal ranked list of animals, birds, and insects from smallest to largest; classification by leg count — two legs (birds), four legs (goat, cat, dog, cow), six legs (ants, grasshoppers), eight legs (spiders); drawings in four categories.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students write the names of all animals, birds, and insects from smallest to largest, and draw and name creatures categorised by number of legs (p. 81–82)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students write a ranked list of creatures from smallest to largest, compare with a partner, then draw and name creatures in four leg-count categories (two, four, six, eight), building a class combined list.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can express a personal connection to a specific living being through drawing and writing, giving reasons rooted in observation and relationship.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Students' chosen favourite animal, bird, insect, or plant; drawn portrait; written reasons — beauty, behaviour, usefulness, emotional connection; gallery sharing; variety of choices across the class as evidence of biodiversity in students' environments.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students identify their favourite animal, bird, insect, or plant and write about why they like it (p. 81)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students draw their favourite living being with colour and write three to five sentences of reasoned personal connection, then share in a gallery format, celebrating the diversity of choices.

assessment_items.question_text: Asha's grandmother told her that when she was young, she kept a goat at home. Asha's family now keeps a parrot. What does this show about families and animals?

options.label: A
options.text: Animals choose which family to live with on their own.

options.label: B
options.text: Different families at different times can have different animals living with them.

options.label: C
options.text: Families always keep the same animals as their grandparents did.

options.label: D
options.text: Only wild animals can live in homes.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. This item tests whether students grasped the intergenerational and family-to-family variation in human-animal relationships discussed through the chapter's opening section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe relationships between their families and living beings in their immediate environment, drawing on personal and intergenerational experience.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

what_each_option_reveals.C: Indicates the student missed the idea of change over time and intergenerational variation — confusing the story of Asha's grandmother with a rule that all families repeat the same pattern.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Indicates a misconception that only wild animals belong outside homes, contradicting the chapter's opening exploration of both invited and uninvited creatures sharing human spaces.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Indicates a confusion between animal agency in the wild and the chapter's focus on human choices and family practices in keeping or welcoming animals.

assessment_items.question_text: Ravi does not like lizards and gets scared when he sees one at home. What are two things Ravi could think about or do that show he understands why the lizard visits his home?
expected_elements: States a reason the lizard comes — for example, to find insects to eat, for warmth, or for shelter.
Suggests a response that does not harm the lizard — for example, opening a window for it to leave, staying calm, or moving to another room.
assessment_items.annotation: A complete response gives one reason for the lizard's presence and one non-harmful response. Accept any ecologically plausible reason and any response that avoids killing or injuring the creature.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can articulate reasons why living beings share human spaces and reflect on a range of human feelings and responses toward them.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

expected_elements: A plausible ecological reason for the uninvited creature's presence — warmth, food (insects), shelter, water.
A non-harmful behavioural response — opening a window, waiting for it to leave, not disturbing it, moving away calmly.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya filled in the table in her textbook with animals she spotted near her home. She wrote: crow — on the roof; ant — in the kitchen; frog — in the garden. What was Priya doing?

options.label: A
options.text: Counting how many legs each animal has.

options.label: B
options.text: Listing only the animals shown in the textbook picture.

options.label: C
options.text: Observing and recording living beings in her immediate environment with the place where she saw them.

options.label: D
options.text: Writing a story about imaginary animals.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. This item checks whether students understand the purpose of the Find out recording task — observation linked to location — as distinct from copying from the textbook or counting legs.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record living beings in their immediate environment, noting the name and location of each.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.D: Indicates the student confused a personal observation record with creative writing — missing the grounded, real-world observation purpose of the task.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Indicates the student did not grasp that the task asked for creatures beyond the textbook picture — a key distinction in the Find out exercise.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Indicates confusion between this observation-and-location task and the later leg-count classification task from the Let us reflect section.

assessment_items.question_text: In the story of Shambhu and his father, a monkey eats a mango and throws away the seed. Shambhu's father says this helps the forest. Explain TWO ways in which the mango tree helps animals and ONE way in which animals help the mango tree.
expected_elements: One way the mango tree helps animals — for example: provides fruit as food, gives shelter or nesting places, gives shade.
A second way the mango tree helps animals — for example: provides wood or medicine (for humans who are also animals in the broadest sense), or a second form of shelter.
One way animals help the mango tree — seed dispersal: the monkey (or another animal) carries and drops the seed, allowing a new mango plant to grow in a new place.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full marks for any two distinct, plausible benefits the tree gives animals and the seed-dispersal benefit animals give the tree. The seed-dispersal answer is the key ecological insight from the story and must be present for full credit.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain the mutual relationships between plants and animals using examples drawn from a story and a diagram.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

expected_elements: A first way the mango tree benefits animals — food (fruit), shelter, shade, or nesting.
A second distinct benefit the tree gives animals.
The seed-dispersal benefit — monkey or animal drops the seed, a new tree can grow — as the way animals help the mango tree.

assessment_items.task: Draw your own web of living-together. Put yourself in the centre of the page. Draw a line to each plant or animal you depend on — and each one that depends on you. On every line, write a short label telling what flows along that line (for example: 'gives milk', 'I water it', 'gives shade', 'spreads its seeds').
assessment_items.scaffold: Start by asking yourself: What did I eat or drink today that came from a plant or animal? Which creature at home needs me to feed or water it? Is there a tree or plant near my home that gives me something? After you draw your web, count the lines going OUT from you (things you give) and lines coming IN to you (things you receive). Are there more in one direction?
format_of_output: A labelled diagram (web) with the student at the centre
At least four lines to different plants or animals
A one- or two-word label on each line describing the relationship
assessment_items.annotation: Look for genuine personal connections — a student in a coastal community may include fish; a student from a farming community may include a bullock or rice plant. All regionally varied answers are acceptable and equally correct as long as the relationship label is plausible. A strong web has lines in both directions — giving and receiving — not only one way.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent their personal relationships of mutual dependence with plants and animals through a labelled diagram.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can visualise mutual dependence as a two-way web rather than a one-directional list, using personal and local examples.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold guides students through self-questioning about food, care, and benefit. A student who answers the scaffold questions but does not draw them as a web has completed only part of the task.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: four or more distinct plants or animals; labels in both directions (giving and receiving); at least one creature or plant that the student gives something to. Weak: only one or two connections; all lines in the same direction (only receiving); generic labels like 'food' without specifying what.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle to draw may write a list with arrows instead of a diagram. Students who cannot write labels may use picture symbols with a key. Students from any region may use locally relevant plants and animals.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: A web diagram makes the structure of mutual dependence visible in a way that a written list cannot — the student can literally see how many connections run in each direction.

assessment_items.question_text: A cow lives with a farming family. The family gives the cow grass, water, and a shed to sleep in. The cow gives the family milk every morning. Which of the following best describes this relationship?

options.label: A
options.text: Both the family and the cow benefit from each other — they need each other.

options.label: B
options.text: Only the cow benefits — the family gives everything away.

options.label: C
options.text: Only the family benefits — the cow gets nothing useful.

options.label: D
options.text: The cow and the family do not have any relationship with each other.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is C. This item tests the central concept of mutual dependence introduced in the 'We Need Each Other' section. The cow-and-family relationship is used as an accessible, concrete anchor.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe specific ways in which humans, animals, and plants provide for each other's needs, forming a circle of mutual dependence.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

what_each_option_reveals.C: Indicates the student sees the relationship as one-directional (human benefits only), missing the 'We Need Each Other' concept of what the animal receives.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Indicates the student sees the relationship as one-directional in the opposite direction — recognising the cow's needs but not the milk the family receives.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Indicates the student has not engaged with the idea of interdependence at all — treating the human and animal as separate with no connection.

assessment_items.question_text: Meena chose to observe a sparrow that visits her window every morning. She watched it for several days and filled in her observation frame. Write THREE things Meena might have written down about the sparrow, using the observation questions from the activity.
expected_elements: An observation about the sparrow's movement — for example: hops along the window ledge, flutters its wings quickly, pecks at grains.
An observation about the sparrow's sounds — for example: makes a chirping or twittering sound, calls loudly in the morning.
An observation about the sparrow's behaviour — for example: came alone or with two others, pecked at food and flew away, bathed in a puddle nearby, something surprising it did.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any three observations drawn from the structured categories in the activity: movement, sound, companions, feeding, sleeping, social behaviour, or something surprising. Regionally varied sparrow behaviour descriptions are all acceptable.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe a familiar animal closely and record its behaviour, movement, and sounds using a structured set of questions.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

expected_elements: A movement observation — how the sparrow moves its body, wings, or legs.
A sound observation — what call or sound the sparrow makes.
A behaviour observation — what the sparrow was doing (eating, resting, interacting with others, or something unexpected).

assessment_items.task: Write a short story about an animal or bird you have watched carefully. Give your story a title. Include: what the creature looks like; where and when you first saw it; how it moves; what sounds it makes; one thing it did that surprised or amused you.
assessment_items.scaffold: Think about your creature. Close your eyes for a moment and picture it. Now open your eyes and answer these questions in your writing: What does it look like — colour, size, shape? Where exactly did you see it — on a roof, in a tree, in your kitchen? How does it move — does it hop, dart, glide, creep? What sound does it make? What is the most interesting thing you saw it do?
format_of_output: Three to five sentences of written description
At least one detail about movement and one detail about sound
assessment_items.annotation: The student may write about any animal or bird they have personally observed — there is no single correct creature. Accept vivid, specific writing about any locally observed animal. A strong response includes at least one sensory detail (sound, movement, or appearance) and one moment of personal response (surprise, amusement, wonder). Regionally varied creatures are all acceptable and equally correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present their observations of a living being through a written descriptive account that includes behaviour, movement, sound, and personal response.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can translate close observation into a coherent written account that goes beyond listing facts to include personal response and vivid detail.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold uses visualisation to help students retrieve sensory detail from memory. A student who answers each scaffold question in sequence will produce a complete response. Watch for students who list facts without any sense of the creature being alive.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: a title; specific sensory details about movement and sound; a genuine moment of personal response (surprise, amusement, wonder); the creature feels real and observed, not invented. Weak: generic statements ('it is a nice bird'); no movement or sound detail; no personal response; fewer than three sentences.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find writing difficult may draw their creature and label its features, then write one sentence for each label. Students may write in their home language if that is the classroom norm and translate key words.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Titled short story or descriptive paragraph
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: A story format (rather than a list or table) encourages students to integrate their observations into a living account that reflects genuine engagement with the creature.

assessment_items.question_text: In the Busy Ants experiment, three foods were placed in a line: sweet (sugar), fried (papad), and cooked (chapati). Before the experiment, students made guesses. After watching, Rohan found that almost all ants went to the sugar first. (a) What kind of step did Rohan do BEFORE watching the ants? (b) What did Rohan's result tell him about what ants prefer?
expected_elements: Names the step before watching as making a guess or prediction (about which food ants would choose, how many would come, what they would look like, etc.).
States that ants preferred the sweet food (sugar) based on the observation — most ants went to the sugar first.
assessment_items.annotation: Award credit for any accurate description of prediction as the pre-observation step, and for any statement that correctly reads the result (ants preferred sweet food). The second part requires the student to draw a conclusion from the observation, not merely restate it.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can perform a simple prediction-and-observation inquiry, recording what they expected and what they actually saw, and discussing the difference.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Identification of the pre-observation step as making a guess or prediction — the student recognises that inquiry begins with a question and a hypothesis before watching.
A conclusion drawn from the result — ants preferred sweet food; most ants chose the sugar — showing the student can read an observation as evidence, not just describe what happened.

assessment_items.task: Think of an animal, bird, insect, or tree that you know well. Mime it for your class to guess — show how it moves, what it does, or how it grows. After your mime, explain in two sentences: What did you have to know about this creature to mime it well?
assessment_items.scaffold: Before you mime, think: How does this creature move its body — does it fly, creep, hop, sway, dart? Does it do something special — build a nest, spin a web, open its petals? Show that with your body. After the class guesses, tell them: 'I had to know that this creature...'
format_of_output: A bodily mime performed in front of the class or a small group
Two spoken or written sentences explaining what knowledge of the creature the mime required
assessment_items.annotation: The mime is the primary output — the two sentences are a reflection on it. A strong performance shows a recognisable feature of the creature (not just random movement) and the reflection names at least one specific thing the student needed to know (e.g. 'I had to know that a snail moves very slowly and keeps its shell on its back'). Any creature from any region is acceptable.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can express their knowledge of living beings through bodily mime, demonstrating awareness of distinctive movements and characteristics.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can translate knowledge of a living being's distinctive features into a physical performance that others can recognise, and then articulate what specific knowledge the performance required.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold focuses students on two things: movement/action (how does it move?) and a distinctive behaviour (what does it do?). A student who shows both in the mime is demonstrating applied knowledge, not guessing.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: the mime is recognisable without verbal clues; the two-sentence reflection names a specific biological or behavioural feature; the student links knowledge to performance ('I had to know that...'). Weak: the mime is generic (just flapping arms for any bird); the reflection is vague ('I had to know about it').
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who are reluctant to perform alone may mime in pairs. A student with physical limitations may draw the creature's key movement on the board and describe it verbally.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Performance task (physical mime) with spoken reflection
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Mime requires the student to encode knowledge of a living being into bodily action — a mode of expression that reveals understanding that written tasks cannot access, and that is central to Activity 3 of this section.
OPEN_TASK.observation_rubric: The teacher watches for: (1) a distinctive feature of the creature shown through body position or movement — not just general animation; (2) consistency — the student maintains the creature's characteristic pace or action throughout; (3) the spoken/written reflection names at least one specific feature the student needed to know to perform the mime.

assessment_items.question_text: In Valparai, Tamil Nadu, school children and teachers welcome the Grey Wagtail every winter with posters and sweets. Why do you think this tradition is important — for the people AND for the bird? Write your answer in four to five sentences.
look_for: Recognises that the tradition strengthens the community's caring relationship with a migratory bird across seasons.
Notes a benefit for the people — joy, a sense of connection to nature, a reason to celebrate, keeping a tradition alive.
Notes a benefit for the bird — or an awareness that welcoming attention may help protect the bird's habitat or safety in the area.
Shows an understanding that human care and natural events can be linked in a community practice.
Writes in connected sentences with a clear personal viewpoint, not just a list.
assessment_items.annotation: This is an evaluative item — there is no single correct answer. A strong response reasons about the two-sided value of the tradition (people and bird) and connects it to the chapter's theme of harmony. Accept any plausible reasoning, including region-specific examples the student draws on for comparison. Award credit for coherent argument, not for a single correct fact.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe a community cultural practice connected to the natural world and explain the relationship between human care and seasonal natural events.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

look_for: The student names what the tradition does for the community — builds a bond with nature, creates a shared celebration, keeps cultural memory alive.

The student reasons about how the bird might be affected — protected, welcomed, safe from harm — or honestly acknowledges uncertainty about the bird's experience while still valuing the human practice.
The student uses the idea of harmony or mutual care from the chapter, not just a description of what happens.
The response is four to five connected sentences with a clear viewpoint, not bullet points.
The student may compare the Valparai tradition to a practice in their own region — this comparative reasoning is a marker of strong understanding.

assessment_items.task: Think of one living being — a plant, animal, bird, or insect — that you would truly like to care for. Write its name and complete these four sentences: (a) I like looking at ___ because ___. (b) ___ makes me feel happy/calm/excited because ___. (c) This living being needs ___ to survive. (d) I would like to take care of it by ___.
assessment_items.scaffold: Choose a real living being that you have actually seen — not an imaginary one. For sentence (c), think about what this creature eats, where it lives, and what it needs to be safe. For sentence (d), think of one real thing you could actually do — not something very big, just one small action.
format_of_output: Four completed sentences with the name of a real living being
Sentence (c) includes at least one specific need of the creature
Sentence (d) includes one specific, actionable care behaviour
assessment_items.annotation: Any real plant, animal, bird, or insect is acceptable. Regionally varied choices are equally valid. The key markers are: the creature is real and named; the need in sentence (c) is specific and plausible; the care action in sentence (d) is genuinely actionable by a child — watering a plant, leaving grain out, not disturbing a nest. Generic or impossible care actions ('I will build a forest for it') should be gently redirected.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can articulate personal reasons for caring about specific living beings and express a sense of responsibility toward them.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can move from personal emotional connection to a creature to a specific, actionable care behaviour — the behavioural disposition the chapter aims to develop.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold steers students to focus on realistic need and realistic action. Watch for students who choose impossible or very vague care actions — redirect them to something they could actually do this week.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: a named real creature; a specific plausible need (e.g. 'needs clean water and insects to eat'); a specific child-sized care action (e.g. 'I will leave a small bowl of water near the window each morning'). Weak: a creature named but no real need stated; a care action that is too large or vague to be actionable.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students may draw the creature alongside their sentences. Students who struggle with sentence frames may say their answers aloud to the teacher or a partner, who scribes. Any regional creature is acceptable.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The sentence frame format scaffolds personal reflection into an externally readable form while allowing genuine individual variation in the creature chosen and the care action described.

assessment_items.question_text: Sona is classifying animals by the number of legs. She writes: ant — six legs; spider — eight legs; sparrow — two legs; dog — four legs. Which animal has been placed in the WRONG group?
assessment_items.annotation: All four classifications are correct — this item tests whether students can verify a classification rather than simply recall. Since all are correct, the intended pedagogical move is for the student to check each one and confirm accuracy. If this item design (all-correct MCQ) is not supported by the platform, replace with: 'Which of the following correctly classifies an animal by its number of legs?' with one incorrect option such as 'Ant — four legs' as a distractor. Award full credit to any student who correctly identifies that all four are correctly classified and explains why.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify living beings by an observable physical feature — number of legs — and order familiar creatures by relative size.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.A: If a student marks this as wrong, it indicates they do not know that insects have six legs — a core classification fact from the leg-count activity.
what_each_option_reveals.D: If a student marks this as wrong, it indicates they do not know that spiders have eight legs — confusing arachnids with insects.
what_each_option_reveals.C: If a student marks this as wrong, it indicates they do not know that birds have two legs — possibly confusing with four-legged mammals.
what_each_option_reveals.B: If a student marks this as wrong, it indicates they do not know that dogs are four-legged — the most familiar example in the chapter.

assessment_items.task: Draw and colour your favourite living being — an animal, bird, insect, or plant. Give it a name label. Then write three to five sentences explaining: (a) why you chose this living being, (b) something interesting about how it moves, eats, or behaves, and (c) one way it helps other living beings — or one way you help it.
assessment_items.scaffold: Look at your drawing. Ask yourself: Why does this creature or plant feel special to me — is it beautiful, funny, useful, gentle? What have I actually seen it do? Who does it help — does it give food to other animals, does it give shade, does it spread seeds? Or: What do I do for it — do I water it, feed it, protect it?
format_of_output: A coloured drawing with the creature's or plant's name labelled
Three to five written sentences covering personal reason, an interesting behaviour or feature, and one relationship to another living being
assessment_items.annotation: Any living being — plant, animal, bird, or insect — is acceptable. Regionally varied choices are equally correct and should be celebrated. The key markers are: the drawing is labelled; the written sentences go beyond 'it is nice' to include a behavioural or relational detail; the third sentence (c) shows awareness of the creature's role in the web of life. Generic or purely aesthetic responses should be noted but not penalised — prompt the student to add one relational detail.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can express a personal connection to a specific living being through drawing and writing, giving reasons rooted in observation and relationship.

competency.competency_text: Identifies needs of plants, birds, and animals, and how they can be supported (water, soil, food, care)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can move from personal aesthetic or emotional preference to a reasoned account of a living being's behaviour and its role in the wider web of life — the culminating synthesis of the chapter.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold moves the student through three layers: personal feeling, observed behaviour, relational role. A student who answers all three is demonstrating the chapter's full arc from feeling to knowing to caring.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: a labelled drawing; personal reason that is specific (not just 'it is nice'); a behavioural or ecological detail that shows real observation; a relational statement that shows the creature or plant as part of a web. Weak: drawing without label; reasons limited to appearance; no mention of the creature's relationship to other living beings.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students may use regional languages to label their drawing. Students who find writing difficult may draw and speak their three sentences aloud to the teacher. Any creature — including very small or 'unglamorous' ones like ants, worms, or weeds — is equally valid and should be affirmed.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Combining drawing with writing allows students to demonstrate understanding through two modes simultaneously — visual and verbal — making the assessment accessible to learners with varying writing confidence while still producing a written record.
